body:
Reading through the [code](https://github.com/celery/celery/blob/e812c5780b4006516116f059ab498e1f043bdd50/celery/backends/base.py#L174-L175), I see that the `errback` is designed to be run inline if it has a function signature that accepts more than one arg.  Naturally, the system is unable to examine the function signature of a task if that task is not in its codebase, which is where the problem lies.

I'd be curious to learn _why_ Celery was designed to handle errors synchronously. Doesn't this violate the advice for [pursuing granularity](http://celery.readthedocs.io/en/latest/userguide/tasks.html#granularity) when writing tasks?  Additionally, it causes errors such as above.  Or maybe I'm missing something?  If I'm correct about above, how would the maintainers feel about a PR to schedule the `errback` as a task if the above error occurs?  Unfortunately, it will be impossible to distinguish between old-style signatures that only accept a single task id arg and new-style signatures that accept the request, exception, and traceback. If there's a work-around for this that would allow us to support both (or if we could ditch support for old-style signatures), please let me know.  Maybe a user should be able to include this detail as an `option` in the errback signature?

As an aside, the documentation around this topic seems a bit hard to follow.  It is correctly documented, however it's done so in the [Chains documentation](http://docs.celeryproject.org/en/latest/userguide/canvas.html?highlight=link_error#chains):

> The worker won’t actually call the errback as a task, but will instead call the errback function directly so that the raw request, exception and traceback objects can be passed to it.

However, in the [Linking (callbacks/errbacks) documentation](http://docs.celeryproject.org/en/latest/userguide/calling.html?highlight=link_error#linking-callbacks-errbacks) it's described differently:

> You can also cause a callback to be applied if task raises an exception (errback), but this behaves differently from a regular callback in that it will be passed the id of the parent task, not the result. This is because it may not always be possible to serialize the exception raised, and so this way the error callback requires a result backend to be enabled, and the task must retrieve the result of the task instead.

Is there a difference between the errback mentioned in the Chains documentation and the errback mentioned in the Linking documentation?

issue.body:
### Proposed changes in this pull request

This PR includes the Cadasta Platform backend for calling and tracking asynchronous operations. The Cadasta Platform codebase is intended to be only an interface for asynchronous tooling, it will not contain code for the actual asynchronous operations.  Currently, this PR includes some example tasks and an example worker to help with testing. The example tasks and workers will be removed or fixed-up before this code makes its way into `master`.

#### Goals

The design goal of this system was to allow us to create workers that embrace _(buzzword alert!)_ microservice principals. This means that the workers should ideally be:

* independently deployable
* small, granular, able to be created by a familiar developer within a week or two
* decoupled from the inner-workings of the Cadasta Platform 

This is an implementation of the planning done in this document: https://docs.google.com/document/d/169fK4G9NkgUulCzs9aHND7aN0GwUKVIP2QPJMi3Jejk/edit

### How to Test

Below are instructions of how to run this on your development machine. The system can be tested locally, without the use of SQS.

#### RabbitMQ

To run the code locally, you must install and start a RabbitMQ Server on your Vagrant vm: `sudo apt-get install rabbitmq-server`. The server should start automatically, you can verify this by running `sudo service rabbitmq-server status`.

_Question: Will we want to include this on the standard CadastaPlatform vagrant machine? Perhaps this could be a flag in the Vagrantfile?_

#### Worker-Boilerplate

The Worker-Boilerplate directory that has been added to the cadasta-platform project represents an external worker that will be running, processing tasks asynchronously. Before merging to `master`, the boilerplate codebase is intended to be spun off into its own repository to be used for quickly developing workers. I've included it in this branch to simplify getting it onto the CadastaPlatform vagrant machine and to assist with testing.

To run on your development machine:

1. Setup virtualenv: `virtualenv /vagrant/worker-boilerplate/env`
1. Activate virtualenv: `source /vagrant/worker-boilerplate/env/bin/activate`
1. Install requirements: `pip install -r /vagrant/worker-boilerplate/requirements.txt`
1. Start worker: `/vagrant/worker-boilerplate/start_worker -l INFO`

_Question: Will we want to include our completed workers on the CadastaPlatform vagrant machine? Perhaps this could be a flag in the Vagrantfile?_

#### Result Consumer

As tasks start, run, and complete, updates about the tasks' state are encoded as messages and placed into the ResultQueue by the workers. The ResultConsumer reads from this queue, updating the DB to reflect the state of the tasks. This will be running as a process on one/many CadastaPlatform Webservers.

To run on your development machine:

1. Install new CadastaPlatform requirements: `pip install -r /vagrant/requirements/common.txt`
1. Run ResultConsumer: `celery -A tasks worker -l INFO`

In effort to minimize race-conditions, this codebase uses `.update()` calls rather than using `.get()` to fetch an instance, changing the instance, and then calling `.save()` to persist the changes.

#### Scheduling Tasks

Now we can schedule tasks to be run on the workers. The system works as such:

* [_Stub_ task functions](https://github.com/Cadasta/cadasta-platform/blob/async/task-tooling/cadasta/resources/tasks.py#L4-L6) should be written to represent any task available to the CadastaPlatform. These functions provide structure around the tasks' signatures so that improperly called tasks throw exceptions when they're scheduled on the webserver rather than when they are executed on the worker. Additionally, the `BackgroundTask` model's `type` field validates against the names of all stub-tasks written in the CadastaPlatform codebase (any task located in a `{module}/tasks.py` file should be autodiscovered when the CadastaPlatform starts up). These stub-functions comes at the price of introducing some coupling between the task producer (the CadastaPlatform) and the task consumers (the workers). This seemed appropriate, as some structure around what input the asynchronous tasks expects should exist _somewhere_. If we ever enter into a situation where we want the capability of adding and using new asyncronous workers and tasks without ever updating the CadastaPlatform (e.g. we could schedule tasks via the Cadasta API and the Cadasta Platform would not need to have any knowledge of what tasks are available or not, it would simply enter the tasks in the queue), then we can remove the validation of the `BackgroundTask.type` field.
* When a stub-task is scheduled, appropriate `BackgroundTask` instances are [created automatically via a signal](https://github.com/Cadasta/cadasta-platform/blob/async/task-tooling/cadasta/tasks/signals.py#L7-L47) to log the created task. The `BackgroundTask` model is intended to only record Celery tasks. Creating a `BackgroundTask` instance does NOT schedule a task (I originally started with a design where the `BackgroundTask` model controlled the task scheduling, however I opted to instead decided to switch the authority to the Celery task tooling when I realized that the Celery task code was more complicated than the tooling around the Django model and trying to make the model mimic the abilities of the Celery tasks proved to be an unnecessary large amount of work.)
* Routing tasks to specific queues is controlled via the `CELERY_TASK_ROUTES` value in the `config.settings.default` settings file. The system is set up so that only the CadastaPlatform is responsible for routing tasks to separate queues. For this reason, the `queue` property is set on all tasks that are in a chain (more on chaining below) before they are scheduled (otherwise it would be up for the workers to route followup tasks, which would fail unless the workers knew of all available queues and tasks within our system).

##### Calling

Celery has many ways to call and execute tasks.

The most basic way to call a task is using the `.delay()` method:

```python
from resources.tasks import hello

# Using delay places the task into the queue
hello.delay('Cadasta!')
```

There are some interesting options to control some meta-details around scheduling a task, including `countdown`/`eta`, `expires`, and `retry`. [Documentation](http://docs.celeryproject.org/en/latest/userguide/calling.html?highlight=countdown#basics)

More complex workflows can be written using [Celery's Canvas tooling](http://docs.celeryproject.org/en/latest/userguide/canvas.html). Currently, only the `chain` operation has been tested and is officially supported.

```python
from resources.tasks import hello, email_msg
from celery import chain
chain(
    # First we'll call the 'hello' task with the argument "Cadasta!". Calling
    # .s() on a task create a task 'Signature', which is basically a task bound
    # to provided arguments and options.
    hello.s('Cadasta!'),

    # The 'hello' task's output will then be passed as the first argument to
    # the 'email_msg' task. We set the 'to_address' argument ahead of time.
    # This is our recommended pattern of doing a followup-task, such as emailing
    # a user when their data export is complete. In this example, we've also set a
    # 'countdown' parameter which causes the 'email_msg' task to wait 5 seconds
    # after the previous task completes before it executes. This could be useful if
    # we had a need to wait a few moments to ensure that the file would be available
    # throughout our system (for some reason) before sending the email.
    email_msg.s(to_address='hello@cadasta.org').set(countdown=5),
)()
```

The `BackgroundTask` instances created from this scheduling will have their appropriate `parent` and `root` relationship fields populated.  Additionally, the `immutable` fields are populated to reflect whether or not the task accepts the output of the previous task as an argument (a developer could use `.si()` rather than `.s()` to prevent a task from accepting its parent's output).

### Running in Production

#### SQS Queues

The CadastaPlatform is set up to use SQS when running with the `config.settings.production` configuration. It is important that the ResultQueue be FIFO (this is not as important for all other queues). Assuming that the AWS credentials associated with the machine/user running the CadastaPlatform has the appropriate permissions, queues will be set-up automatically as needed by Celery (either when the first task is scheduled or when a worker is instructed to reqd from the queue.) It would be useful to experiment to find what are the bare-minimum amount of permissions needed to run the async codebases.

#### Environment Variables

The CadastaPlatform, ResultConsumer, and the Worker-Boilerplate expect a `QUEUE_PREFIX` environment variable to be set. This allows us to keep `staging`, `production`, and `demo` queues separate by prefixing queue names with a string. For example, if we are to use a queue named `platform-staging-result.fifo`, the `QUEUE_PREFIX` should be set to `platform-staging` and the queue name set to `result.fifo` (the hyphen between the two is added automatically).

#### ResultConsumer

The ResultConsumer should be run as a daemon process (likely on the CadastaPlatform web servers). You start the ResultConsumer by starting up a standard Celery Worker. This allows us to lean on any [Celery Worker configuration](http://docs.celeryproject.org/en/latest/userguide/workers.html) that we may desire (autoscaling, concurrency, etc). One strange part of the ResultConsumer's design is that Result Messages aren't encoded in the same format as standard Task Messages. For this reason, we can't instruct the celery worker to point to the Result Queue (ie don't use `-Q result.fifo`), instead it awkwardly should point to either no queues (which will set it to consume from the default queue, `celery`) or some null queue (`-Q _`) that is gauranteed to have no actual task messages.

### When should this PR be merged

Anytime as this PR does not aim to be merged to `master`

### Risks

The method used to get task results from the Worker machines to the CadastaPlatform is to have all Worker machines configured with a `result_backend` of `rpc://`. By design, [the RPC backend](http://docs.celeryproject.org/en/latest/internals/reference/celery.backends.rpc.html#celery-backends-rpc) works by placing all Task results into a separate queue for every client. This allows the client machines to fetch the results of a task (blocking, if desired.) By overriding the `reply_to` option for all tasks, we instruct the RPC backend to return all results to a single queue that can be consumed by our ResultConsumer. Breaking the standard RPC workflow is pretty uncharted territory and may have negative impacts (for example, some advanced workflows such as creating a `group` of tasks may make use RPC results.)

Secondly, it doesn't seem that Celery was written with decoupled codebases in mind. The documentation makes little mention about _where_ operations task place (i.e. task producer vs task consumer.) It seems that the library often makes the following assumptions about both the Task Producers and Task Consumers:

* both have access to the task functions (i.e. running the same codebase)
* both have access to a ResultBackend for storing/retrieving task results (e.g. SQL DB, Redis)
* both have knowledge of how to route tasks based on the tasks' names

Because of the above, I ran into a number of problems when building out this tooling. For example, it seems that error-back tasks (tasks that only run if a previous task fails) don't fit in with our design (see celery/celery#4022). Unfortunately, the documentation is either missing or incorrect in a number of places, making finding these issues a bit of a try-and-see process.

Overall, I think Celery's good parts greatly outweighs the bad parts and these are issues that we can work around/resolve. The Celery codebase doesn't move too quickly so these things will take time and exploration on our part (which is why this PR installs both Kombu and Celery off of their `master` branches.)

Finally, I see that there is a Documentation checkbox at the bottom of this PR's checklist. Should this information be documented anywhere? A lot of it is basically "read the Celery docs" however there is some specific Cadasta-related info (like using RPC and the ResultConsumer).

### Follow-up actions

My next steps are to port the current Export code to a worker process. This will lean on using the [TempScopedTokens](https://github.com/Cadasta/drf-temporary-permissions-token) and the PaginatedAPI that had been created previously.

---

### Checklist (for reviewing)

#### General

- [ ] **Is this PR explained thoroughly?** All code changes must be accounted for in the PR description.
- [ ] **Is the PR labeled correctly?** It should have the `migration` label if a new migration is added.
- [ ] **Is the risk level assessment sufficient?** The risks section should contain all risks that might be introduced with the PR and which actions we need to take to mitigate these risks. Possible risks are database migrations, new libraries that need to be installed or changes to deployment scripts.

#### Functionality

- [ ] **Are all requirements met?** Compare implemented functionality with the requirements specification.
- [ ] **Does the UI work as expected?** There should be no Javascript errors in the console; all resources should load. There should be no unexpected errors. Deliberately try to break the feature to find out if there are corner cases that are not handled.

#### Code

- [ ] **Do you fully understand the introduced changes to the code?** If not ask for clarification, it might uncover ways to solve a problem in a more elegant and efficient way.
- [ ] **Does the PR introduce any inefficient database requests?** Use the debug server to check for duplicate requests.
- [ ] **Are all necessary strings marked for translation?** All strings that are exposed to users via the UI must be [marked for translation](https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/1.10/topics/i18n/translation/).

#### Tests

- [ ] **Are there sufficient test cases?** Ensure that all components are tested individually; models, forms, and serializers should be tested in isolation even if a test for a view covers these components.
- [ ] **If this is a bug fix, are tests for the issue in place?**  There must be a test case for the bug to ensure the issue won’t regress. Make sure that the tests break without the new code to fix the issue.
- [ ] **If this is a new feature or a significant change to an existing feature?** has the manual testing spreadsheet been updated with instructions for manual testing?

#### Security

- [ ] **Confirm this PR doesn't commit any keys, passwords, tokens, usernames, or other secrets.**
- [ ] **Are all UI and API inputs run through forms or serializers?**
- [ ] **Are all external inputs validated and sanitized appropriately?**
- [ ] **Does all branching logic have a default case?**
- [ ] **Does this solution handle outliers and edge cases gracefully?**
- [ ] **Are all external communications secured and restricted to SSL?**

#### Documentation

- [ ] **Are changes to the UI documented in the platform docs?** If this PR introduces new platform site functionality or changes existing ones, the changes must be documented in the [Cadasta Platform Documentation](https://github.com/Cadasta/cadasta-docs).
- [ ] **Are changes to the API documented in the API docs?** If this PR introduces new API functionality or changes existing ones, the changes must be documented in the [API docs](https://github.com/Cadasta/api-docs).
- [ ] **Are reusable components documented?** If this PR introduces components that are relevant to other developers (for instance a mixin for a view or a generic form) they should be documented in the Wiki.

issue.title: Different behavior on group's link/link_error usage
issue.body:
## Steps to reproduce
```
g = group(sig1, sig2)
g.link(sig3) # links to sig1
g.link_error(sig4) # links to sig1
g.apply_async(link=sig3) # raises TypeError
g.apply_async(link_error=sig4) # raises TypeError
```

## Expected behavior
```
g.link(sig3) # should rise TypeError exception with referencing to chord
g.link_error(sig4) # should rise TypeError exception with referencing to individual error handlers, or silently apply link_error to each task
```

issue.title: Using a class based task as errback results in AttributeError '_header_'

milestone.title: v4.3
milestone.description: The last version to support python2

issue.body:
## Checklist

- [X] I have included the output of ``celery -A proj report`` in the issue.
      (if you are not able to do this, then at least specify the Celery
       version affected).
[celery-report.txt](https://github.com/celery/celery/files/1456808/celery-report.txt)
- [ ] I have verified that the issue exists against the `master` branch of Celery.

## Steps to reproduce
Create a tasks file:
```
from celery import Celery,Task
celery = Celery('tasks', broker='redis://localhost:6379/6',backend='redis://localhost:6379/6')

@celery.task
def ErrTask1(req):
    print('failure')

class CustomTask(Task):
    def run(self,var):
        print('running %s' % var)
        if var == "err":
            raise Exception("err")
CustomTask = celery.register_task(CustomTask())

class ErrTask2(Task):
        def run(self):
                    print('failure')
ErrTask2 = celery.register_task(ErrTask2())

```
start celery with it:
`celery worker -A tasks:celery -l info`

Start a python shell and start the CustomTask with an error callback:

```
from tasks import CustomTask,ErrTask1,ErrTask2
a = CustomTask.apply_async(['err'],link_error=ErrTask1.s())
a.result
b = CustomTask.apply_async(['err'],link_error=ErrTask2.s())
b.result
```
## Expected behavior
When running with ErrTask1 as error callback ( the one with the decorator) we get the expected result:
```
>>> a = CustomTask.apply_async(['err'],link_error=ErrTask1.s())
>>> a.result
Exception(u'err',)
```
## Actual behavior
When running with ErrTask2 as error callback ( the one that is defined classbased) we get the Attributeerror:
```
>>> b = CustomTask.apply_async(['err'],link_error=ErrTask2.s())
>>> b.result
AttributeError(u"'ErrTask2' object has no attribute '__header__'",)
```
It seems the changed behaviour on the error callback in celery 4 has something to do with it. The class based tasks miss some attributes which doesn't seem to be an issue for normal execution but only for the error callback. Probably there is a difference in initialization between `celery.register_task()` and the decorator.

Workaround is to define the error callbacks with the task decorator.

I am facing this issue with celery 4.1.
I have 2 celery workers attached to one broker, but without sharing the code.

    current_app.send_task('gsclient.run_task', kwargs={'task_id': task.id}, queue=queue_name,
                          link=complete_task.subtask(kwargs={'task_id': task_id}),
                          link_error=complete_task.subtask(kwargs={'task_id': task_id}),
                          )

When the task finishes without error - `link` is called and executed. In case of error `link_error` is not called with the stack trace from the first post of this thread.

In my case workaround will be to wrap the task to handle all exceptions, but return error code.
This might have been addressed by commit https://github.com/celery/celery/commit/bc366c887f194a3ff1f99671d9742a525a066339 : "*Added support to bind=True task as link errors*"
